newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Judges parade for last time before HK handover.
newsitem.headline: Judges parade for last time before HK handover.

text.p: Hong Kong's judges bedecked in all their ceremonial finery of wigs, robes, hose and gaiters paraded in Hong Kong at the start of the legal year for the last time before the British colony becomes a part of China.

Silks shimmered, shoe-buckles glimmered and heads covered in horsehair wigs handmade in London bowed as the doleful notes of the British anthem God Save the Queen rang out across Hong Kong's Roman Catholic Cathedral.
Later came an honour parade on the waterfront drawn from what remains of the British garrison which is winding down ahead of the handover of Hong Kong to China at midnight on June 30.
With just 169 days before the final curtain on more than 150 years of colonial rule, the relics of the British empire are fading fast in Hong Kong -- but judges wigs may be an exception.

"I don't know. Some people want to keep the wigs. Some people want to get rid of the wigs. Some people want to keep the robes and some people want to get rid of them," High Court Judge Justice Anthony Rogers told Reuters.

"In fact when we speak to Chinese judges, they want to have some kind of formal robes rather than the military uniform they wear at the moment. So I suspect we will keep some kind of robe but whether it will be exactly the same, I don't know."

Hong Kong faces a shortage of judges in the delicate countdown period and is seeking suitable local candidates from the ranks of the legal community. Many lawyers say they are reluctant to give up lucrative private practice for the bench.

Acting Chief Justice Noel Power -- elevated when former Chief Justice Ti Liang Yang stepped down late last year to run unsuccessfully for Hong Kong's post-colonial leadership -- said the 171-strong judiciary was 17 judges short.
He said another High Court judge and 13 lower court judges planned to step down this year.
"Ten have retired who may not otherwise have done so," Power said, admitting the shortages were a cause for concern but remained manageable.

China has promised Hong Kong it can retain its English-style common law and capitalist systems for 50 years after the handover, but many people fret that Beijing may seek to erode judicial freedoms further down the road.
